book: How Search Decides What You See
author: Aaron Tay

scenes.title: A million papers, one question
scenes.claim: Scale makes careful comparison expensive
scenes.narration: Imagine a universe of papers, and one very particular question. Reading every paper carefully for every search would take too long. Search systems divide the work: find promising candidates quickly, then spend more effort comparing the survivors. Welcome to Chapter nine: reranking and multi-stage retrieval.

scenes.title: Two speeds, two jobs
scenes.claim: Retrieve across the collection → compare the shortlist
scenes.narration: The first stage searches the collection with an indexed method: Boolean, BM25, dense retrieval, learnt sparse retrieval, or another route. Its job is to retain useful candidates within a practical budget. A reranker then scores that shortlist using richer evidence. Only a small part of the collection receives the expensive comparison.

scenes.title: The missing paper cannot come back
scenes.claim: A reranker can reorder candidates; it cannot add an excluded record
scenes.narration: Here is the catch. A reranker receives candidates, not the collection. Our toy paper G is relevant, but never enters the shortlist. No clever second score can bring it back. If several retrievers contribute candidates, their union may widen the pool. Once that pool is fixed, reranking remains inside its boundary.

scenes.title: Better at the top, same candidate pool
scenes.claim: Toy example: top-three precision 1/3 → 3/3; pool recall stays 3/4
scenes.narration: In this toy collection, four papers are relevant. Three reach the shortlist. Before reranking, only one of the top three is relevant. Afterwards, all three are. Precision at three improves, and recall at three improves too. But candidate-pool recall stays three out of four. The missing fourth paper is still unavailable.

scenes.title: Find the stage that lost the evidence
scenes.claim: Coverage → retrieval → candidate budget → reranking → display
scenes.narration: A missing result needs a diagnosis. Was the paper in the searchable collection? Did retrieval find it? Did it survive the candidate budget? Did reranking move it down? Was it below the displayed cut-off? The same empty screen can hide failures at different stages. A stronger reranker fixes only some of them.

scenes.title: A candidate is only the text supplied
scenes.claim: Title, abstract, passage, and full text expose different evidence
scenes.narration: There is also a text boundary. A candidate might be a record, an abstract, or one passage. A reranker comparing abstracts cannot use a detail found only in the full text. More careful scoring means a richer comparison of supplied evidence. It does not create evidence that the model never received.

scenes.title: Every cut-off narrows the view
scenes.claim: Illustrative budgets: 100 candidates → 10 displayed results
scenes.narration: Think of two doors. In our schematic pipeline, one hundred candidates reach the reranker, but only ten results are displayed. Those are different budgets with different consequences. Answer generation may introduce another selection. Unless the system explicitly runs another retrieval, later stages work with the survivors they were given.

scenes.title: Ask about the shortlist first
scenes.claim: Which route? How many candidates? Which text? Which final cut-off?
scenes.narration: When a vendor says it uses AI reranking, ask what supplied the candidates, how many arrived, what text was compared, and how many survived. Then evaluate the whole pipeline on your task. A later stage can spend more computation, but only on records that an earlier stage admitted. Next, we open the comparison machinery.

episodes.title: Three ways to compare a question and a paper
episodes.subtitle: Bi-encoders, cross-encoders, and late interaction

scenes.title: Same topic, different usefulness
scenes.claim: Stated need: judge whether job expectations are unrealistic
scenes.narration: Am I being delulu about getting this job? For this teaching case, the need is to judge unrealistic expectations. One passage addresses that need. Another lists signs of a successful interview. Both sound relevant to job seeking, but they answer different questions. The comparison must preserve the distinction that matters.

scenes.title: Compress first, compare later
scenes.claim: Bi-encoder: independent encoding → pooled vectors → similarity
scenes.narration: A conventional bi-encoder encodes the query and passage independently, usually into one vector each. Passage vectors can be prepared in advance. At search time, the system compares stored representations. That makes collection-scale retrieval practical. But pooling compresses local detail before the passage knows what the query will ask.

scenes.title: Read the question and candidate together
scenes.claim: Cross-encoder: joint token interaction → a ranking score
scenes.narration: A cross-encoder puts the query and one candidate into the model together. Attention can run across their tokens before the score is produced. That makes finer comparison possible: expectations versus interview performance, a qualifier, an entity, or a negation. The score is a learned relevance estimate, not an objective truth.

scenes.title: The relation matters, not just the topic
scenes.claim: Joint encoding can examine how candidate text addresses the need
scenes.narration: Our question turns on whether expectations are unrealistic. The interview passage turns on whether someone performed well. Joint comparison can weigh that difference in what the passage does with the topic. This does not guarantee the preferred ordering. Training, input truncation, and the task's definition of relevance still matter.

scenes.title: The careful pass has a price
scenes.claim: 100 candidates require roughly 100 query–candidate evaluations
scenes.narration: The price is repeated model work. A cross-encoder's candidate representation depends on the query, so it cannot be fully precomputed and reused. One hundred candidates need roughly one hundred pair evaluations, even if they are batched. Affordable on a shortlist can become impractical across millions of records.

scenes.title: Keep the token detail for later
scenes.claim: Late interaction: independent encoding, multiple token vectors
scenes.narration: ColBERT-style late interaction takes another route. Query and document are encoded independently, but token vectors are retained instead of pooling everything into one vector. Document token vectors can be stored in advance. Later comparison keeps more local evidence, at a cost in storage and computation. This arrangement can retrieve candidates or rerank them.

scenes.title: Best token matches, added together
scenes.claim: Invented MaxSim example: 0.90 + 0.80 = 1.70
scenes.narration: Here is the chapter's invented MaxSim example. For each query token, keep its highest similarity to a document token, then add the maxima. Citation contributes zero point nine; benefit contributes zero point eight. The total is one point seven. These are contextual similarities, not word counts. One document token may be best for several query tokens.

scenes.title: The arrangement determines what survives
scenes.claim: One pooled vector · joint encoding · retained token vectors
scenes.narration: The same pretrained model family can support different arrangements. Independent pooled vectors favour efficient reuse. Joint encoding compares the pair in context. Late interaction retains token-level matching evidence. Its alignments show which tokens contributed, not why their vectors were similar. Ask about the arrangement and training, not just the model name.

episodes.title: How to build a useful result list
episodes.subtitle: LLM reranking, diversity, and real pipeline budgets

scenes.title: One candidate at a time
scenes.claim: Pointwise: independent judgements need comparable scores
scenes.narration: A large language model can rerank too. Give it a query, candidate text, and relevance instructions, perhaps about population, method, or study design. Pointwise reranking judges each candidate separately. The work grows with the shortlist, but scores may need calibration. The model does not directly compare competing candidates.

scenes.title: Which of these two is more useful?
scenes.claim: Pairwise: direct comparisons; preferences may be inconsistent
scenes.narration: Pairwise reranking presents two candidates and asks which is more relevant. Direct comparison can reveal subtle differences. But many comparisons may be needed, and preferences can conflict. In our invented cycle, A beats B, B beats C, and C beats A. One comparison does not automatically give a consistent ranking.

scenes.title: Order several candidates together
scenes.claim: Listwise: comparative context, limited by input size and order effects
scenes.narration: Listwise reranking presents several candidates together and requests an ordering. Long lists can exceed the context window, so systems may use sliding windows or repeated partial rankings. Candidate order can influence the result. Here these labels describe judgements at reranking time; classical learning to rank also uses them for training objectives.

scenes.title: An explanation is another output to check
scenes.claim: Evaluate rankings; a plausible rationale does not validate them
scenes.narration: A model can explain its choice in fluent prose. That can make inspection easier, but the explanation is not proof that the ranking is correct. Prompt wording, candidate order, model changes, and sampling settings can affect results. Evaluate the complete pipeline with judged queries, including the evidence that never reached the model.

scenes.title: A good next paper adds something
scenes.claim: Schematic selections: relevance-only A B C; diversified A D E
scenes.narration: A useful list is more than useful items. In the chapter's schematic open-access example, A, B, and C repeat one aspect. D covers disciplinary differences; E examines selection bias. An exploratory list might choose A, D, and E. F is weakly related: being different is insufficient. This illustrates an objective, not a calculated algorithm result.

scenes.title: Similar studies can all matter
scenes.claim: Diversification ≠ deduplication; broader aspects ≠ balanced evidence
scenes.narration: Diversification asks what an item adds to the selected set. Deduplication removes records judged equivalent under another rule. Papers B and C remain distinct studies, even if they share an aspect. A systematic review may need all relevant studies. Diversity-aware selection can hide useful neighbours below a cut-off, and topical variety does not guarantee balanced evidence.

scenes.title: Two documented pipelines, different budgets
scenes.claim: Published PubMed: top 500 reranked · documented Primo: up to 30 → 5
scenes.narration: The chapter makes the budgets concrete. PubMed's published Best Match architecture uses BM25, then LambdaMART on the top five hundred. Results continue below that reranked region. Primo Research Assistant's documented pipeline retrieves through CDI, reranks up to thirty with embeddings, and sends five abstracts to answer generation. These documented architectures illustrate different boundaries, rather than a promise about every future deployment.

scenes.title: Neural retrieval is a whole family
scenes.claim: Dense · learnt sparse · late interaction · neural reranking
scenes.narration: Neural information retrieval is broader than dense retrieval. A model can produce pooled dense vectors, retain token vectors, learn sparse vocabulary weights, or rerank lexical candidates. Learnt sparse expansion can add vocabulary before inverted-index search, so typed-word overlap is not always required. Across every arrangement, inspect the candidate route, budget, supplied evidence, and final selection. Chapter ten asks how multiple retrieval routes combine.
